lyrics:
I asked for a plane that could actually fly
They tossed me a box and walked away
No diagram drawn, no reason why —
just plastic and glue and a rainy day

So I put myself into the parts that I had
forced the wings where they didn't belong
Nobody promised the frame could withstand —
I flew it in secret and called myself strong

Some assembly required, the box declared —
didn't say the job was never done
I built a man from the parts I had spared
called it finished before it was begun

Now every year I bolt another part —
a laugh, a job, a voice that isn't mine
No one ships you a blueprint or a chart —
you learn to hide the seams and call it fine

Some assembly required, the box declared —
didn't say the job was never done
I built a man from the parts I had spared
called it finished before it was begun

The glue never fully dried on these parts
Get near enough and the seams still show
Nobody tells you when you start —
the building never lets you go

Some assembly required, the box declared —
didn't say the job was never done
I built a man from the parts I had spared
called it finished before it was begun

[Interlude - angular unison build]

[Verse 3 - quieter, honest]
Now every year I bolt another part —
a laugh, a job, a voice that isn't mine.
No one ships you a blueprint or a chart —
you learn to hide the seams and call it fine.

[Chorus - flat, matter-of-fact]
Some assembly required, the box declared —
didn't say the job was never done.
I built a man from the parts I had spared,
called it finished before it was begun.

[Bridge - stripped, confessional]
The glue never fully dried on these parts.
Get near enough and the seams still show.
Nobody tells you when you start —
the building never lets you go.

[Final Chorus - fuller, harmonized]
Some assembly required, the box declared —
didn't say the job was never done.
I built a man from the parts I had spared,
called it finished before it was begun.

[Outro - mechanical fade]

[End]

  Approved critic summary: Rose opens with a mumbled false start on 'I'm Old Now,' and that small, deliberate stumble tells you exactly what kind of record this is: nothing performed, nothing smoothed over, just a man taking honest stock.

  Approved critic summary: "A Distant Memory" opens with a counted-off "one, two, three, four" that sets a brisk 4/4 in C major, and from there Rose lets a female vocal float above a clean, roomy groove that leans more toward jazzy indie-pop than any straight ballad.

  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.
- 2026-08-20 — Them Bones (single)
  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.
- 2026-08-30 — Unreasonably Quiet (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.
- 2026-09-12 — Wazoo In Effigy (album)
  Approved critic summary: Michael Anthony Rose’s *Wazoo in Effigy* is inspired by Frank Zappa, which is not quite the same thing as being a Zappa tribute.
- 2026-09-18 — The Grounding Post (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose has spent 2026 moving between sprawling ambition and compressed intimacy, and 'The Grounding Post' lands firmly in the second register, closer in spirit to the quiet honesty of 'I'm Still Here' than to the operatic scale of 'Outlandia.' The track runs 3:29 in F# major, built on dry, close-miked fingerpicking and a baritone vocal that has the stillness of someone writing in the early morning before anyone else is awake.

impression.text: The track opens with a bright piano melody that quickly builds into a driving, high-energy pop-rock anthem. Its emotional atmosphere feels both earnest and theatrical, anchored by a charismatic male vocal performance that soars over the vibrant arrangement. The production is polished and dense, successfully balancing sweeping strings and heavy electric guitars while leaving enough space for the lead vocals to sit clearly in the mix. A defining quality of the song is the explosive transition from its buoyant piano-driven verses into a massive wall-of-sound chorus that gives the track an undeniable stadium-ready feel.

review.review_text: Rose delivers a looser and warmer driving 4/4 in A major at 136 that leans stadium where the script leaned angular. No matter, because the conceit carries it: a childhood plane kit becomes the whole architecture of a self, and the flat, deadpan chorus lands the trick, 'called it finished before it was begun,' with the wry stillness of an early morning admission. The best line is the bridge's plain confession, 'get near enough and the seams still show,' and Rose is smart enough not to oversell it. Not the strangest thing in a strange 2026 catalog, and the arrangement doesn't fully commit to the mechanical unwind the ending wants, but the writing does its job and does it well.
